questions.question: Which TWO factors can affect the cost of Azure resources?

options.text: The Azure region where the resource is deployed
The name you give the resource
The amount of outbound data transfer (egress)
The colour theme of the Azure portal

questions.explanation: Cost factors include resource type, consumption, maintenance, geography (region), network traffic, subscription type and Marketplace purchases.

questions.scenario: You delete an Azure VM but are still charged for storage each month.
questions.question: What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The VM's managed disks were not deleted
options.why: Correct. Disks are separate resources and keep billing.

options.text: Azure charges a permanent fee for deleted VMs
The resource group itself has a monthly cost

questions.explanation: Orphaned disks, public IPs and snapshots continue to incur cost until deleted. Maintenance affects cost.

questions.question: Which tool lets you configure Azure services and see an estimate of their monthly cost before deploying anything?

options.why: Monitor collects telemetry from running resources.

questions.explanation: The pricing calculator estimates costs for planned resources; it does not deploy anything.

questions.question: Which TWO can you do with Microsoft Cost Management?

options.text: Analyse spending with cost analysis views

questions.explanation: Cost Management provides cost analysis, budgets, alerts, forecasts and recommendations.

questions.scenario: Finance needs to see Azure costs split by department and project across many resource groups.
questions.question: What should you apply to resources?

options.text: Tags such as Department and Project
options.why: Correct. Tags let you filter and group costs.
Locks prevent changes; they do not categorise costs.

questions.explanation: Tags are name-value metadata used for cost reporting, ownership and automation.

questions.question: Are tags applied to a resource group automatically inherited by the resources inside it?

options.text: No, not by default. You can use Azure Policy to apply or inherit tags

options.why: No resource type inherits tags by default.

questions.explanation: Resources do not inherit tags by default; Azure Policy can enforce or inherit them.

questions.question: Which service helps an organisation discover, classify and govern data across on-premises, multi-cloud and SaaS sources?
questions.explanation: Microsoft Purview provides unified data governance and risk and compliance solutions.

questions.scenario: All new storage accounts must use secure transfer (HTTPS). Non-compliant accounts must be blocked at creation.
questions.question: What should you use?

options.text: An Azure Policy with a Deny effect

options.why: Locks prevent deletion or changes; they do not validate settings.

questions.explanation: Azure Policy evaluates resource properties and can deny, audit or remediate non-compliance.

questions.question: What is an Azure Policy initiative?

options.text: A group of related policy definitions assigned together

questions.explanation: Initiatives bundle policies to achieve a larger goal, such as a regulatory compliance standard.

questions.scenario: A production database must never be deleted accidentally, but administrators must still be able to change its configuration.
questions.question: Which resource lock should you apply?

options.why: Correct. It allows changes but blocks deletion.

options.text: No lock. Use a tag instead

questions.explanation: Delete locks block deletion; ReadOnly locks block deletion and modification.

questions.question: A user with the Owner role tries to delete a resource that has a Delete lock. What happens?

options.text: The deletion fails until the lock is removed
options.why: Correct. Locks apply to all users, including Owners.

options.text: The resource is deleted because Owners bypass locks
The resource moves to another region

questions.explanation: Locks override RBAC permissions. Someone with rights to manage locks must remove the lock first.
